pr_body:
OSSL_trace_end() should validate that the category it has been passed
by the caler is valid, and return immediately if not.

Fixes #17353

issue_context.title: Potential locking problems due to the inconsistent checking
issue_context.body:
Hi, I found a potential locking problem.

When `category < 0` at line 466, the lock `trace_lock`at Line 473 is not acquired.
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/a935791d54078f43209ffbc1886ac5e68772ce34/crypto/trace.c#L459-L473

The range of `category` is not checked at line 498, lock `trace_lock` could be released without acquiring at line 516?
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/a935791d54078f43209ffbc1886ac5e68772ce34/crypto/trace.c#L493-L516
comments:
The checks of category range are horribly inconsistent here ... and they should all be the same.

The consistent test for not-valid category should be:

`    if (category < 0 || category >= OSSL_TRACE_CATEGORY_NUM)
`

And for valid should be:

`    if (category >= 0 && category < OSSL_TRACE_CATEGORY_NUM)`

Yes a bug that should be fixed, and the range checks should be consistent as per @t-j-h's comment - but the impact of this bug is minimal/negligible. If `category < 0` then `OSSL_trace_begin()` will return NULL. If the caller is using it in accordance with the documentation then `OSSL_trace_end()` should be passed the BIO returned from `OSSL_trace_begin()`. Since that is NULL, it will never hit the unlock code in `OSSL_trace_end()`.

If the caller is using the convenience macros `OSSL_TRACE_BEGIN` and `OSSL_TRACE_END` correctly (as is the case through the OpenSSL code internally) then this bug will never be hit.
Thank you very much for your checking.

review_comments:
It‘s a programming error if the trace groups are not properly nested. Instead of silently ignoring it, I‘d add `if (!ossl_assert(category >= 0))`. (Note that there is already an assertion a few lines below). 

(Disclaimer: this is a quick drive-by comment from my mobile phone, hope I didn’t miss anything)
Hmmm… just read issue #17353. I need to take another look when I‘m back on my computer.

We normally reserve `ossl_assert` and `assert` for catching internal errors. This is actually public API, and so the "bug" would be in the caller and therefore may not be an "internal" error. So, its not clear to me that `ossl_assert` is actually appropriate.
It is not an *assert* context. This is something that can easily happen with a public API.
